Hochwohlgebohrner Herr Insonders Hochzuehrender Herr Lieutenant! Schönen muß ich mir wohl, Ew. Hochwohlgebl. gütiges Schreiben so lange danckbahrlich unbeantwortet gelaßen zu haben, rechnete ich nicht auf ihr gütiges Entschuldigen, so würde es jezt nicht von neuen Wagen Dieselben mit meinen gegenwärtigen zu belästigen.

daß ich Schleßen und Brau verlassen müßen, worinnen beinahe 49 Jahre meist glücklich und froh gelebt, und bei in zu meinen Auffenthalt gewählt, um meine dringünste Geschäfte der Verlust meines Vermögens, hier beßer zu betreiben wenn möglich noch etwas zu retten, wäiIhnen vielleicht nicht gantz unberauß sein Allein noch sind hierzu die Außachten nicht sehr klar, und selbst mein alte gewesener Sachwalter in Posen Hl. Weltzer, der sich jezt auch hier aufhält, der die Polnische Justiz zu können glaubt, hat wenig Hoffnung, das Ausweitige Departement hat sich für mich an den Dresden Huffe verraut, allen auch dieser, will zwar daß die vorher bezahlten

Schulden nachgesucht werden könten, waß aber die Güter selbst betrift, so sucht Er — absehen kein officieller Befehl des Keisers hiezu vorhanden. die damaligen Polnischen Richter zu entschuldigen und die tilsitum friedens articulae so für und hierinnen sein, nicht darauf anwendbahr zu machen.

Der hiesige Franzosische Gesante, bei dem voriges sehr bei meinen Hiersein war, macht mir in der Art hoffnung: daß wenn kein ausdrückliche Keiserliches Befehl hierzu vorhanden, und ich die official Ihm geben könnte, Er sich meine vor, nehmen wolte. Endlich habe ich den selbst vom Sächsischen Hofe, welcher sagt, daß die von Dąbska in desden den Keiser und die zurückgabe der Güter gebeten — So keiselich Majestät bloß der damaligen Pluischen Regierung Ihre Bittschrift zugeschickten Hierauf haben Die Polnsche Commissarien befohlen der am Dąbska die Güter wieder zugeben. Gegenwärtig bin beschäftigt dieses Übersehen gelaßen, und werde sehen in wie weit

der Französische hiesige Gesante, sich dieser Sachen annehmen wird, weide auch nicht verfohlen Ew. Hochwohlgebl. so gleich davon Nachricht gegeben, damit Fr. Hochfürstlich Durchlaucht die ich mich zu Gnaden zu empfehlen bitte davon gleichfals villeicht gebrauch machen könten.

Wie werde die Wohltaten vergeßen so ich durch diesen Fürsten erhilt, meine Anhänglichkeit kann und wird nie sterben.

Ist denn noch keine Sententz aus den ersten Tribunal über des Fürsten Trąbczyner Güter heraus? Hütten Ew. Hochwohlgeb. wohl die Güte mir wißen zu laßen, 1) wenns möglich abschriftlich — waß die Friedens Ruhte feurteilt, und 2t waß die Sententz mit den triebonal besagt hat?

Neues wolle Ihnen gerne mit fielen allein auß in einem Tage hier für gewis ausgegeben. wird den andern bezweiffelt, und den dritten verdrängt eine zweite oft wiedersprechend

die erſten So viel scheint aber doch aus allen hervorzuleuchten, daß man einen baldigen Ausbruch des Krieger in Norden vermutet. Würde es im Abend klar so würde es in Norden brennen sei ist glaube ich der Ableiter. zu Erwaltung einer zütigen Antwort und Verzeihung meiner Nachläßigkeit verharre in der vollkommensten Hochachtung lebenslang Ew Hochwohlgebohren

Michalina z Prusimskich Dąbska, later Miączyńska

mentions_english.display: Michalina z Prusimskich Dąbska, later Miączyńska

translation.en:
217

Right Honourable Sir, most particularly Highly Honoured Sir Lieutenant! Fine [uncertain: Schönen] it must appear of me, to have left Your Right Honourable's kind letter so long unanswered with due thanks; did I not count upon your kind indulgence, I should not now venture anew to burden you with my present one.

That I have had to leave Silesia and Wrocław, wherein I lived nearly 49 years, mostly happy and glad, and have chosen [uncertain: bei in] for my residence, in order better to pursue here my most pressing affairs — the loss of my fortune — and if possible still to save something, will perhaps not be entirely unknown to you. But the prospects in this are as yet not very clear, and even my old former lawyer in Poznań, Mr Weltzer, who is now likewise staying here, and who believes he knows the Polish justice, has little hope. The foreign department has [uncertain: verraut] itself on my behalf to the Dresden [uncertain: Huffe], but this one too, though it will indeed have it that the previously paid

debts might be sought after, yet as concerns the estates themselves, he seeks — [text lost] no official order of the Emperor being at hand for this — to excuse the Polish judges of that time, and to make the Tilsit peace articles, however much they be in favour and herein, not applicable to it.

The French envoy here, with whom formerly [uncertain: voriges] there was much during my being here, gives me hope in this manner: that if no express Imperial order exists for this, and I could give him the official one, he would take my part. Finally I have obtained the same from the Saxon court itself, which says that Dąbska in [uncertain: desden] petitioned the Emperor and begged for the restitution of the estates — that His Imperial Majesty merely forwarded her petition to the then Polish [uncertain: Pluischen] government. Thereupon the Polish commissioners ordered that the estates be given back to Dąbska. At present I am occupied in having this [uncertain: Übersehen] left aside, and shall see how far

the French envoy here will take up these matters; nor have I failed [uncertain: verfohlen] to give Your Right Honourable notice of it at once, so that His Most Serene Highness — to whose grace I beg to be commended — might perhaps likewise make use of it.

How shall I forget the benefactions I received through this Prince; my attachment can and never will die.

Has then still no sentence come out of the first Tribunal concerning the Prince's Trąbczyn estates? Would Your Right Honourable have the goodness to let me know, 1) if possible in copy — what the justice of the peace [uncertain: Friedens Ruhte] adjudged, and 2nd what the sentence with the tribunal has stated?

News I would gladly [uncertain: mit fielen] give you, but what is given out here for certain on one day is doubted the next, and on the third a second, often contradictory, one displaces

the first. So much, however, does seem to shine out of it all, that an early outbreak of the war in the North is presumed. Were it clear in the evening [uncertain: im Abend], then it would burn in the North; that, I believe, is the conductor. Awaiting a [uncertain: zütigen] reply and the pardon of my negligence, I remain in the most perfect esteem, lifelong, Your Right Honourable's

Berlin

the 15th of August 1811

text_english:
217

Right Honourable Sir, most particularly Highly Honoured Sir Lieutenant! Fine [uncertain: Schönen] it must appear of me, to have left Your Right Honourable's kind letter so long unanswered with due thanks; did I not count upon your kind indulgence, I should not now venture anew to burden you with my present one.

That I have had to leave Silesia and Wrocław, wherein I lived nearly 49 years, mostly happy and glad, and have chosen [uncertain: bei in] for my residence, in order better to pursue here my most pressing affairs — the loss of my fortune — and if possible still to save something, will perhaps not be entirely unknown to you. But the prospects in this are as yet not very clear, and even my old former lawyer in Poznań, Mr Weltzer, who is now likewise staying here, and who believes he knows the Polish justice, has little hope. The foreign department has [uncertain: verraut] itself on my behalf to the Dresden [uncertain: Huffe], but this one too, though it will indeed have it that the previously paid

debts might be sought after, yet as concerns the estates themselves, he seeks — [text lost] no official order of the Emperor being at hand for this — to excuse the Polish judges of that time, and to make the Tilsit peace articles, however much they be in favour and herein, not applicable to it.

The French envoy here, with whom formerly [uncertain: voriges] there was much during my being here, gives me hope in this manner: that if no express Imperial order exists for this, and I could give him the official one, he would take my part. Finally I have obtained the same from the Saxon court itself, which says that Dąbska in [uncertain: desden] petitioned the Emperor and begged for the restitution of the estates — that His Imperial Majesty merely forwarded her petition to the then Polish [uncertain: Pluischen] government. Thereupon the Polish commissioners ordered that the estates be given back to Dąbska. At present I am occupied in having this [uncertain: Übersehen] left aside, and shall see how far

the French envoy here will take up these matters; nor have I failed [uncertain: verfohlen] to give Your Right Honourable notice of it at once, so that His Most Serene Highness — to whose grace I beg to be commended — might perhaps likewise make use of it.

How shall I forget the benefactions I received through this Prince; my attachment can and never will die.

Has then still no sentence come out of the first Tribunal concerning the Prince's Trąbczyn estates? Would Your Right Honourable have the goodness to let me know, 1) if possible in copy — what the justice of the peace [uncertain: Friedens Ruhte] adjudged, and 2nd what the sentence with the tribunal has stated?

News I would gladly [uncertain: mit fielen] give you, but what is given out here for certain on one day is doubted the next, and on the third a second, often contradictory, one displaces

the first. So much, however, does seem to shine out of it all, that an early outbreak of the war in the North is presumed. Were it clear in the evening [uncertain: im Abend], then it would burn in the North; that, I believe, is the conductor. Awaiting a [uncertain: zütigen] reply and the pardon of my negligence, I remain in the most perfect esteem, lifelong, Your Right Honourable's

Berlin

the 15th of August 1811

summary_de: Von Sanitz fragt, ob das erste Tribunal über die Trąbczyner Güter des Fürsten schon entschieden hat, und bittet möglichst um Abschriften des Friedensrichter-Urteils und der Tribunalsentenz. Er ist nach Berlin gezogen, um Reste seines verlorenen Vermögens zu retten. Sein früherer Posener Sachwalter Weltzer hat wenig Hoffnung. Vom sächsischen Hof hört er, Polnische Commissarien hätten auf eine Bittschrift von Dąbska befohlen, ihr die Güter zurückzugeben. Man vermute einen baldigen Krieg im Norden.

reading.notes: Von Sanitz writes from Berlin to Triebenfeld, whom he addresses as Lieutenant. He apologises for answering late. He has left Silesia after about 49 years and is in Berlin to try to save his lost fortune. His former lawyer Weltzer has little hope. The foreign department has approached the Dresden court, and the French envoy offers conditional hope. The Saxon court reports that Dąbska petitioned the Emperor and that Polish commissioners ordered the estates returned to her. He asks whether the first Tribunal has given its sentence on the Prince's Trąbczyn estates, and asks for copies of the Friedensrichter ruling and of the tribunal sentence. He adds rumours of war in the North. The text is heavily garbled.
